r2-p11-000: In stage 1, added mass is expected to lower the natural frequency, so the peak frequency should fall under the weight conditions, while in the asymmetric 1-0 changes in amplitude and band energy are expected before any frequency shift. Because indoor temperature/humidity changes are smaller than openLAB's seasonal change, the compensation effect may also be small, so the criterion is whether the trend of improvement (fewer false alarms) is reproduced rather than its absolute size. In stage 2, the added mass exceeds the deck mass (about 243 g), but because the weights sit near the supports, the effective mass on the first mode is smaller than it appears. The first natural frequency should therefore fall clearly but not by as much as the mass ratio, and the actual size will be fixed by measurement after assembly. The focus of observation is ordering rather than detection: we check whether the anomaly score and ratio increase monotonically as conditions within the same damage type become more severe (M0→M500→M1000, B0→B1→B2), which must hold for the anomaly score to serve as a severity indicator for inspection priority. Comparisons between different types are excluded from validation because their physical references differ and no correct answer can be defined; in operation they are presented only as a relative ranking of departure from normal. Bolt loosening is expected to bring a small drop in natural frequency accompanied by secondary changes such as harmonics and wider peaks. In short, we test the hypothesis that mass is distinguished by the size of the frequency shift and bolts by the combination of accompanying features, and also check whether the reverse shift of 1-0, interpreted as scatter in stage 1, disappears with automatic excitation and whether the compensation effect is reproduced in the three normal cells where only the environment changed.
r2-p11-002: In the preliminary test the first peak was observed at about 22.6 Hz, so the base analysis bands were reset to 0–12, 12–25 and 25–50 Hz. The mass change of 1-0 was detected by the multi-feature anomaly score, raising the exceedance rate to 29.7%. In the humidity-change segment the false-alarm rate fell from 17.5% uncompensated to 9.1% with temperature/humidity compensation. This 8.4-point reduction is actually larger than openLAB's 0.38 points, because humidity can be changed strongly indoors, so the false-alarm rate before compensation was high and there was correspondingly more room to reduce it. The stage-1 results are presented in two tables and Figures 4 and 5; the first table aggregates by condition and the second gives per-model metrics over the whole evaluation segment, so their populations differ and they are not directly comparable. In Figure 4, check whether the mean anomaly score of the weight conditions (1-0, 1-1) rises above normal (0-0); in Figure 5, check whether the metrics improve as compensation steps are added.

r2-p12-003: With the temperature/humidity-compensated model, all 840 damage windows exceeded the threshold (recall 100%), and there were 4 false alarms among the 90 normal evaluation windows (4.4%). All four occurred in the simultaneous temperature/humidity (To·Ho) block; the 4/30 (13.3%) in the table below is the same four alarms counted against that block's 30 windows. All 1,380 windows of the 27 conditions were valid, none discarded. The measured normal first natural frequency is 101.0 Hz, and the anomaly threshold is a reconstruction error of 5.6064. The mean anomaly scores in the table are absolute values on the same scale as this threshold, while the ratios (2.2) in the text and Figure 6 are those values divided by the threshold. Each damage group in the table sums the three environment blocks (105 windows each), and the distribution over all 27 cells is shown in Figure 6. The peak shifts in the table are far larger than the gradual drop expected in 3.3 (e.g., −64.4%), and there are even reversals where more severe damage gives a smaller shift (M1000·B1 −19.8%). This does not mean the natural frequency actually fell that far. A structure has several vibration modes at once, and the peak frequency reads only the single tallest peak; when damage changes the strength of each mode, the tallest peak jumps from the original 101 Hz mode to a lower mode (mode switching). The value therefore jumps instead of falling continuously, and since which mode becomes tallest is not monotonic in the size of the damage, reversals are natural (detailed interpretation in 3.5).
r2-p12-016: Over 5 repeated seeds, both compensated models kept 100% recall for every seed, while the uncompensated AE varied between 96.2% and 99.3% (interpretation in 3.5). The ROC-AUC of the three models is 0.994–0.996.

r2-p13-011: The stage-1 results matched the expected physics. Under loading on both sides (1-1), the mean peak frequency fell by 8.9%, exactly as expected from the natural frequency falling as mass increases (f = (1/2π)√(k/m); with the same stiffness k, a larger mass m lowers f). The main contributing band also moved from 0–12 Hz to 12–25 Hz, where the first resonance lies, supporting the same interpretation. Under loading on one side (1-0) the peak
r2-p13-012: rose by 0.8%, but this is within the scatter of manual tapping and is not a meaningful change. Instead, the amplitude and band features responded, and the exceedance rate jumped from 4.5% (normal 0-0 windows) to 29.7% (1-0). This confirms the design assumption that a small asymmetric mass change must be caught by an anomaly score combining several features, not by a single frequency. The remaining problems were that damping in the foam board blurred the resonance peak, burying small frequency changes in the peak width, and that manual tapping varied in force and timing every time, enlarging the scatter of normal measurements even without damage. In unsupervised detection, which flags anything outside the normal scatter, a wide normal scatter means correspondingly small damage is missed, so these two problems became the improvement targets of stage 2.
r2-p13-013: The stage-2 results show four things.
r2-p14-000: First, standardizing the excitation with a machine fixed the normal baseline. After the auto-tapper was introduced, the peaks of the 60 room-temperature normal evaluation windows
r2-p14-001: converged on a single value, 101.0 Hz, with a standard deviation of 0.0 Hz. This means the variation in force and timing of manual tapping, a problem in stage 1, disappeared, and the 0.8% reverse peak shift attributed to that variation in stage 1 did not reappear. Second, the 27 conditions were separated almost completely. The figures are as in the table in 3.4; the key point is the gap between normal and damage. The median ratio was 0.003–0.038× for normal windows and 5.8–73.7× for damage windows, a gap of more than a hundredfold (Figure 6). The tails did not separate completely, however: one normal window in the heated block spiked to 15.9×, and the weakest damage window reached only 2.0×. In actual operation, therefore, decisions are based on the exceedance rate over consecutive windows rather than a single window. The severity ordering was clean for mass: the ratio grew monotonically from 5.8× for M500 to 22.6× for M1000 in all three blocks. For bolts, loosening even one bolt saturated the score at tens of times the threshold, so the ordering held only in the low-severity range, and in the no-change block B1's 71.5× even exceeded B2's
r2-p14-003: Third, the composition of reconstruction-error contributions points to the type of damage (Figure 7). In windows with loosened bolts, the 40–80 Hz band-ratio residual accounted for 76–90% of the reconstruction error; in windows with added mass, amplitude/energy features such as log RMS accounted for 73–80%. Read in reverse, this becomes an operating guideline: if the 40–80 Hz band ratio dominates an alarm's contributions, suspect damage to boundary conditions such as bolted joints first; if the amplitude/energy features dominate, suspect a change in load (mass) and start the inspection there. That the two groups appeared side by side at 51% and 46% in combined mass + bolt windows supports this. It is not a diagnosis that fixes location and type, but it sets the starting point for the follow-up precision inspection. Meanwhile, the peak frequency swung far more than expected for both mass and bolts because of mode switching (3.4) (bolt B1 −36.6%, B2 −60.4%), showing that the stage-1 conclusion — detect by combining several features rather than relying on a single peak — remained valid in stage 2.
r2-p14-004: Fourth, the role of temperature/humidity compensation changed from stage 1. Thanks to stepwise heating and continuous humidification, the normal training data already covered 22.4–39.9 °C and 48.9–79.0% humidity, environmental change rarely caused false alarms even without compensation, and there was no room for a reduction like that in stage 1. Instead, the benefit of compensation appeared as more stable detection: when training was repeated with 5 seeds, the recall of the uncompensated model fluctuated between 96.2% and 99.3%, whereas the compensated model reached 100% with all five.
r2-p14-005: The largest share of the performance gain came from feature normalization. Because amplitudes differed by up to about 40× between conditions, standardization with stage 1's raw features was dominated by amplitude, giving a recall of only 21.3% (in a reanalysis applying the raw features directly to the stage-2 data) and 0% for mass windows, whereas switching to log and ratio normalization raised it to 100% on the same data.
r2-p14-006: The remaining 4 false alarms are all windows near 39.9 °C, the hottest point of the heating — a limitation of approximating the structure's temperature with air temperature and humidity alone; improvements are discussed in 4.2. r2-p15-001: Using only low-cost commercial parts (ADXL355Z, DHT22, Raspberry Pi), this system demonstrated the target performance of first-stage screening, prior to precision inspection, on the 27-condition matrix of a laboratory model. The temperature/humidity-compensated model caught all 840 damage windows and raised only 4 false alarms among 90 normal evaluation windows, recording window-level recall of 100%, a false-alarm rate of 4.4%, F1 0.998 and ROC-AUC 0.996. Whereas in stage 1 it was a system that was usually right when it alarmed but often missed damage (precision 0.888, recall 0.234), in stage 2, after standardized excitation and a redesign of feature normalization, it became a system that alarms accurately without misses.
r2-p15-002: The value of temperature/humidity compensation appeared in three different forms. Where training had not seen enough environmental variation, it reduced false alarms directly (stage 1: 17.5%→9.1%; openLAB: 1.90%→1.52%); in stage 2, where environmental coverage was secured, it appeared as detection stability, keeping recall at 100% regardless of the random seed. On top of this, contribution analysis of the reconstruction error changes the quality of an alarm. With a system that gives only an anomaly signal, an inspector cannot know what to examine, but this system also shows which features increased the error. In stage 2, the 40–80 Hz band-ratio residual accounted for 76–90% of the contribution for bolt loosening and the amplitude/energy residuals for 73–80% for mass change, so the alarm alone was enough to narrow the direction to a boundary anomaly or a load change. It does not fix the location or type of damage, but it provides a practical clue as to where the follow-up precision inspection should start. The within-type severity ordering held in every block for mass, providing grounds for using it as an inspection-priority indicator, and for bolts it held only in the low-severity range B0→B1, before the score saturated. On the model side, a nonlinear Autoencoder with an 8–3–8 hidden structure, built on log/ratio-normalized features, replaced stage 1's linear PCA implementation, but the dominant factor in the performance gain was the feature representation rather than model capacity. All of these figures, however, come from short-term indoor model experiments. Traffic loads, seasonal cycles and long-term drift on a real bridge have not yet been experienced, so any judgment on practical use must wait until the field validation in 4.2 has been passed.
r2-p15-004: Future improvement focuses on a single goal: field validation on a real bridge. What could be checked on a model was checked in stage 2, so the remaining question is whether the same performance holds in a real operating environment. For the sensor's own measurement performance we rely on prior work [1], which validated modal measurement of real structures with the same ADXL355 family; instead, short measurements at several candidate bridges will compare the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of ambient vibration, and the bridge with the sharpest resonance peak will be chosen. Candidates are limited to pedestrian overpasses (Class 3 scale) that recently passed a precision inspection, so the inspection record supports the assumption of a normal state at the start of measurement; a single node with a waterproof enclosure, power and communications is installed under the center of the main span, and excitation switches to the ambient vibration produced by pedestrians and wind.
r2-p15-005: Next is quantifying the compensation effect in the real environment. After training the regression, Autoencoder and threshold on site with the first week of normal data following installation, two to three weeks of undamaged continuous monitoring will compare the false-alarm rates of the uncompensated and compensated models side by side, measuring with our own system's data how much temperature/humidity compensation reduces false alarms under the daily temperature range and weather changes of a real bridge. Upper limits for the window-level false-alarm rate and for the number of consecutive-window false alarms will be declared before monitoring begins; procedures for monthly retraining and threshold updates and the measurement of baseline drift on sensor remounting will be established in this period, and the limitation of approximating structural temperature will be addressed by adding a deck surface-temperature sensor. Validation over all four seasons is a long-term task to be continued through permanent operation of the node.
r2-p15-006: Finally, detection power will be checked. Because damage cannot be inflicted on a real bridge, reversible controlled disturbances — a known mass placed at a designated position with the cooperation of the managing authority — will be inserted midway through and at the end of monitoring. The size of the disturbance will be calculated in advance to match the change in natural frequency that real damage produces according to the literature (a few percent), and two to three load levels will be used to check whether the stage-2 severity ordering is reproduced. Passing these three steps would provide the validation basis for moving, via comparison with periodic inspections, multi-node expansion and a review of damage localization, toward a continuous screening tool for small and medium bridges.
